claims.text: Adding 2–5 at% aluminum to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
Adding 2–5 at% aluminum will promote formation of a continuous, slow-growing, protective Al2O3 scale.
A refractory alloy composed primarily of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W lacks enough protective oxide-forming elements to inherently form a protective scale during high-temperature exposure.
Aluminum segregates to the alloy surface at high temperature.
Surface-segregated aluminum reacts with oxygen to form a dense, adherent Al2O3 layer.
The Al2O3 layer acts as a diffusion barrier that reduces oxygen ingress.
Reduced oxygen ingress prevents further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
Formation of the Al2O3 barrier enhances structural integrity under extreme-temperature conditions.
At 1100°C in air for 3 hours, the aluminum-modified alloy will have significantly lower weight gain than the untreated alloy.
At 1100°C in air for 3 hours, the aluminum-modified alloy will exhibit less spallation or scale cracking than the untreated alloy.
Under the same exposure conditions, the untreated refractory high-entropy alloy will form less protective oxide scales.
Less protective oxide scales on the untreated alloy will result in higher oxidation rates.
Aluminum contents below the proposed optimal range may be insufficient to form a protective alumina scale.
Aluminum contents outside the proposed optimal range may cause detrimental phase changes.
The proposed mechanism may not operate at significantly lower temperatures or under different reactive-gas compositions.
